description: Hi! I'm Rishi S S, an AI engineer at Ascendion from Chennai, India. I like building things that solve real problems, and space and Earth-science data is one of my favourite places to do that.
summary:
Martian Map is a web app that helps the first astronauts on Mars plan and carry out a Marswalk safely while doing real science along the way. It layers data from NASA and ESA spacecraft (Viking, Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Express, and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers): orbital imagery, thermal and spectral maps, terrain models, geologic maps, rover photos and radiation measurements, plus live space weather, all in one map of a specific route instead of the regional and global views existing tools offer.

An astronaut picks a science goal, such as the boxwork ridges Curiosity studied on Mount Sharp or the "leopard spot" rock at Cheyava Falls in Jezero crater, and the app plans a walking route that steers around ground steeper than 15°. Every step is checked against both suits' oxygen, battery, cooling water and CO2 scrubber, against daylight, radiation dose and a live solar-storm go/no-go, with a point of no return and the time to shelter. The crew can see the ground first in real rover photos and a 3D flyover, follow the route live on a tablet or a helmet-visor HUD, and print an Apollo-style cuff checklist.

It matters because the first human missions to Mars will depend on hyper-local, trustworthy maps: one wrong slope, one late turn-back or one unexpected solar particle event is a safety risk, and a well-chosen stop is a scientific discovery.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Martian Map is a planning and guidance tool for one Marswalk (EVA), from choosing a science target to walking back to the habitat. It answers the questions a crew asks before stepping outside: Where do we go to do the best science? Which way is safe? Do our suits have enough oxygen, power and cooling for it, with a reserve? Is the Sun quiet today? What does the ground look like when we get there? And once outside: Am I on the right path, and when must I turn back?

1. Choose a science goal and a place. Five ready-made science EVAs sit where rovers and orbiters have studied closely: the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp (Gale crater, studied by Curiosity in 2025), the "leopard spot" rock at Cheyava Falls and the Three Forks sample depot (Jezero crater, Perseverance), a fresh crater that exposed clean water ice (Arcadia Planitia, MRO HiRISE) and the hot-spring silica of the Columbia Hills (Gusev crater, Spirit). Each states the science question, the stations with their tasks, the kit to carry and the time each takes. Any other walk can be planned too: search 2,052 IAU place names, type coordinates, pick a landing site or click on the map.

2. Plan a safe route. For each leg an A* search on the terrain model routes around ground steeper than 15° (a minute on such ground counts like six on the flat) and never over slopes beyond 25°, then straightens the path where the ground allows. It uses the 20 m HiRISE terrain of Gale and the 20 m CTX terrain of Jezero, and the 200 m HRSC/MOLA blend everywhere else. The result reads like a maps app: turn-by-turn directions, an elevation profile coloured by slope, and the steep stretches marked.

3. Check every step against the crew and the conditions. Every 50 m of the route is turned into metabolic effort with the Pandolf load-carriage equation, scaled to Mars gravity using measured reduced-gravity walking costs and to the extra effort of a pressurised suit. Effort then becomes oxygen, CO2-scrubber, cooling-water and battery use, for both suits of a buddy pair, since the pair is only as far from empty as the emptier suit. Work time at each station and legs driven on a rover are included. The plan is then checked against:

  • the reserve each supply must keep, with a "point of no return" past which you can no longer walk back to the start;
  • the Apollo-era 10 km walk-home limit;
  • daylight and sun angle at every stop (Mars24 algorithm);
  • the radiation dose of the walk, from Curiosity's RAD measurements;
  • a live space-weather go/no-go, built from NASA DONKI (flares, particle events, CMEs forecast to reach Mars) and NOAA GOES data and worked out for where Mars actually is around the Sun, not where Earth is;
  • carried load against body mass, pace, dust-devil hours and the dust-storm season.

The verdict comes in plain words ("Safe single EVA, back by 12:43" or "Not enough cooling water in EV2's suit") with the reason, and every figure links to one of 59 published sources in the app's Science tab.

4. Understand the ground. Orbital science layers, each with a legend in plain language: THEMIS night infrared and TES thermal inertia (firm rock versus soft dust and sand), TES dust cover, CRISM and OMEGA water-formed minerals, THEMIS chloride salts, HiRISE ice exposures, recurring slope lineae (marked as planetary-protection keep-outs) and active gullies, the USGS global geologic map, and the detailed USGS 1:75,000 geologic map of Jezero, where you can click any of its 1,308 mapped areas to read its description and interpretation. Every route gets a "Science along the way" card: the rock units it crosses (contacts are where a geologist samples both sides) and the detections within 2 km, each addable as a science stop with one click.

5. See it before you go. "Ground view" opens the nearest real rover stop within 3 km: Navcam frames laid out around 360° by the direction the camera pointed, full-colour Mastcam-Z/Mastcam frames, and WATSON/MAHLI microscope close-ups; at Cheyava Falls that means the leopard-spot rock itself. A 3D globe streams the same NASA terrain and imagery, with the route draped on the ground and the rovers' real traverses, and a chase camera flies along the planned walk so the crew can rehearse it.

6. Walk it. Mars has no GPS, so live guidance takes position fixes from the suit or rover navigation (tap the map or type coordinates) and snaps each one to the route: distance to the next turn, off-route and wrong-way alerts, steep ground ahead, estimated arrival, supplies left (updated from the suit's own readings) and a turn-back alert when the rest of the walk would eat into the reserve. The same guidance runs on a tablet layout or a full-screen helmet-visor HUD with a compass tape pointing to the next station, suit gauges, the EVA clock, radiation dose so far, space-weather status and the light-time to Earth.

7. Take it with you. A printable Apollo-style cuff checklist carries a shaded-relief traverse map, the station timeline, the supplies expected at each station and the turn-back rule for each. Any area, with the route raised on it, can be exported as a 3D-printable relief model for briefing the crew around a table, as Apollo crews did.

HOW IT WORKS UNDER THE HOOD

A Python (FastAPI) server samples the elevation models (local 20 m DTMs, a streamed 200 m global DEM, the MOLA grid as fallback), runs the route search, builds the terrain profile of each route and answers the science queries, and proxies NASA's rover-image and space-weather services with caching. The heaviest imagery (the global 5 m CTX mosaic and HiRISE 25 cm) is re-encoded once as small WebP tiles; because CTX and HiRISE are black-and-white cameras, the server colours each tile with the Viking colour of the same ground, so close-ups still look like Mars. Broken source tiles are filled from the next zoom level, and failed requests retry, so the map never shows holes. The browser app is plain JavaScript with Leaflet for the 2D map, CesiumJS for the 3D globe and three.js for a short cinematic intro (galaxy to solar system to Mars, whose globe unrolls into the map). It is deployed as a Docker container on Google Cloud Run at https://martianmap.us.

BENEFITS

  • One place, one walk: everything a crew needs for a specific route (terrain, geology, minerals, ice, photos, supplies, Sun, radiation) instead of separate regional and global tools.
  • Decisions, not just data: go/no-go verdicts with their reasons, a point of no return, a turn-back alert and the time to shelter.
  • More science per hour outside: targets along the route are suggested and can be added as stops, with tasks and kit already listed.
  • Trustworthy: every number is cited, every layer says where it comes from, and the 3D view never flies closer than its terrain data can honestly show.
  • Works everywhere: a browser on a laptop, tablet or phone; a visor HUD; and paper (the cuff checklist) for when screens fail.

INTENDED IMPACT

For the first crews and their mission planners, Martian Map is a prototype of the hyper-local, decision-ready map a Marswalk needs. Today it can brief crews in Mars analog missions on Earth, help scientists compare exploration zones around landing sites, and let students and the public explore Mars with real mission data in plain language. The next steps are live rover and weather feeds, more 1 m terrain models, and testing the HUD and live guidance with crews in analog missions.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • It borrows proven ideas from Apollo (cuff checklists, relief models, the 10 km walk-back rule, buddy pairs) and rebuilds them from Mars data.
  • "Street View for Mars": rover photos laid out around 360° from their camera-pointing records.
  • Space weather judged from Mars's own position around the Sun, including the side of the Sun that Earth cannot see.
  • Greyscale orbital close-ups coloured with real Viking colour, so detail and colour both come from data.
  • A helmet-visor HUD, a live "am I on track?" guide for a planet without GPS, and 3D-printable route models.
  • Orbital mineral and ice detections turned into one-click science stops.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

  • Astronaut safety first: slope limits, supply reserves for both suits, turn-back and point-of-no-return, time to shelter, radiation dose, solar storms, daylight, dust devils, and planetary-protection keep-outs at recurring slope lineae.
  • Mobility in a suit: effort from body mass, carried kit, slope and Mars gravity; slower walking speed; station work; rover legs.
  • Mars realities: no GPS (manual position fixes), a signal delay to Earth of about 3 to 22 minutes each way (decisions made on site), local solar time and seasons.
  • Honesty about data: each result names its terrain source and resolution and warns where only coarse data exists; the 3D camera never goes closer than the data supports.
  • Usability: one main action per screen, plain-language explanations, keyboard access, visible focus, reduced motion, and a phone layout that keeps the map and directions on screen together.
  • Reliability and speed: small cached tiles, the 3D engine loaded only when needed, fallbacks when a NASA service is down, retries for failed tiles.
  • Openness and cost: only free and open data and open-source software; free hosting credit and domain from the Space Apps global offers; the code is public on GitHub.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Server: FastAPI, uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, Pillow, tifffile, LERC, httpx.
  • Browser: Leaflet (2D map), CesiumJS (3D globe), three.js (intro), Chart.js (elevation profile), the Web Audio API (the intro's synthesised soundtrack).
  • Hosting: Docker, Google Cloud Run (Space Apps global offer credit), domain martianmap.us (Space Apps global offer), GitHub.
  • Video: Playwright and ffmpeg to record the demo and tour from the live site.
  • Hardware: none needed beyond a computer or phone with a browser; a 3D printer is optional for the relief models.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for code, disclosed in the README and in the app.
  • Source code: https://github.com/RISHI-1453/NASA_Space-Apps_Challenge_Martian_Map
  • Live site: https://martianmap.us/
